label: graphql-directives-auth-en
top_ai_sentences:
Resolver-level auth is the better choice when the
logic gets complex, like allowing an edit only for the owner or org members.

If you need finer control, use
@hasPermission to check specific actions like post:delete instead of broad roles.

They're
also useful when a field should be visible only to the object owner, regardless of the viewer's role.
Use custom auth directives when fields inside the same type need different access levels.

If either check fails, the field returns an error or
null, depending on your config.

Admins still get through; that's intentional so support
staff can pull user data.
They work, but each subgraph has to implement the directive on its own.

For example, a user reads their own email but not
someone else's, an admin sees every field, and a public field needs no auth.
Every GraphQL field can have its own authorization rule.

The original resolve function is preserved, or defaultFieldResolver is used when
the field has no custom resolver.

Public fields should still work without a token, or your landing page
and public queries will break.
@owner checks the parent object's authorId against context.user.id.

Send queries with different user tokens and check that protected fields return errors or null based on the
role.

They also aren't the best choice if your rules are too complex to express declaratively, like multi-tenant
org membership.
Directives work well for straightforward field-level rules.
Test different roles by sending queries with different context.user values and asserting who can see what.

You can also use a directive to limit query cost:



This gives you a basic cost guard without touching resolvers.

The gateway won't re-run subgraph
directives.
Stack the directives: @auth(requires: EDITOR) @owner.

When stacking directives, document the evaluation order so your team doesn't
get surprised by a short-circuit.

If that
passes, @owner verifies the user owns the resource.
Checking auth in both resolvers and directives creates duplicated logic, so pick one approach.
Declare auth in the schema so rules stay visible and easy to audit.

If your app has roles like
admin, editor, and viewer, and you need field-level granularity, directives handle that cleanly.
Role-based auth with @auth is the most common starting point.

El gateway no re-ejecuta
las directivas de los subgrafos.
Cacheá las búsquedas de permisos para evitar consultar la base de datos en cada resolver.

Las directivas andan bien para reglas simples a nivel campo.

La auth a nivel resolver es la mejor opción
cuando la lógica se pone compleja, como permitir una edición solo para el dueño o miembros de la misma
organización.

Campos anidados como user.email también
necesitan directivas.

retorna error o null, según tu configuración.

La directiva @auth verifica el rol primero.

Si tu app tiene roles como admin, editor y viewer y

@hasPermission para verificar acciones específicas como post:delete en lugar de roles anchos.

Verificar auth en resolvers y directivas al mismo tiempo genera lógica duplicada, así que elegí un enfoque.
